frameworks.name: Wealth Spending Archetypes
frameworks.definition: Four distinct spending profiles that reveal personal values and trajectory: rich people prioritize time, poor people buy stuff for status, ambitious people buy skills, lazy people buy distraction.

frameworks.name: Identity-Spending Alignment
frameworks.definition: Personal identity shifts require congruent spending and calendar allocation; misalignment between stated goals and actual budget/calendar reveals the true identity being formed.

claims.text: Rich people buy time. Poor people buy stuff. Ambitious people buy skills. Lazy people buy distraction.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Your future results are determined by where you invest your money and calendar time today. When examining a person's bank account and accomplishments at year-end, their spending patterns and calendar allocation explain the discrepancy between stated goals and actual outcomes.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: We vote with our dollars and time about the person we want to become; these votes compound into identity through repeated reinforcement.

claims.text: Identity shifts require spending and calendar changes to precede behavior change, not follow it. The timing sequence matters: a person must first allocate money and time to the new identity, then the behaviors and outcomes align.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Person wants to adopt a new identity
Identity shift is meaningful enough to warrant resource allocation
claims.mechanism: Allocating scarce resources (time, money) to an identity makes that identity real by forcing daily choices that reinforce it.
bounded_by: Does not apply to aspirational statements without resource commitment
Does not explain identity formation when spending and calendar remain unchanged

claims.text: Most people fail their annual goals because they say they want results but never allocate the budget or calendar time required to achieve them. Stating a goal without spending change is insufficient; the person continues voting for their current identity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Person has not reallocated budget or calendar
claims.mechanism: Goals require visible resource commitment; without spending or time changes, the nervous system and identity do not update.

claims.text: If future outcomes matter enough to pursue, they matter enough to pursue today, not next year. Delaying investment decisions (saying 'I will start next year') reveals that the goal is not sufficiently meaningful.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Person is setting a future start date
claims.mechanism: Delay signals that the goal lacks sufficient pull; meaningful goals have no delay switch.

claims.text: Ambitious people invest in skills and knowledge; the spending category itself (skills vs. consumption) indicates whether a person is building wealth-producing capacity or consuming wealth.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Skills generate future income; stuff consumes present income. The type of spending determines whether capital compounds or dissipates.

claims.text: Your bank account and calendar at year-end are a financial and temporal report card on your priorities, not on your circumstances. Blame, excuses, and external attribution mask the fact that your spending choices created your outcomes.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: A person is evaluating past-year results
claims.mechanism: Personal agency operates through spending and time allocation; examining those two variables reveals what the person truly prioritized.

claims.text: Entrepreneurs receive market feedback that social relationships withhold; this unfiltered feedback is the fastest personal development vehicle available.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Person is receiving real market feedback
claims.mechanism: Market feedback is objective and consequences are immediate; social relationships have incentive to be polite rather than truthful.
bounded_by: Does not apply in sheltered entrepreneurship without real customers
Does not apply if feedback is defensive rather than inquisitive

claims.text: Current you is the only version of you that will ever experience life. Delaying investments in growth for a future version is a form of deferred living.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: The present is the only moment of subjective experience; investments made now compound into future capacity.

examples.text: Alex Hormozi's father's original advice: Rich people buy time. Poor people buy stuff. Ambitious people buy skills. Lazy people buy distraction. This four-part taxonomy reveals spending patterns as identity markers and predictors of future wealth trajectory.

Two young girls (approximately 9-10 years old) were being helped by a sales associate at Sephora. The associate told them, 'Now that you guys are women, you need to start budgeting for makeup because you're going to be spending money on this every month.' The girls became excited, grabbed paint brushes, and went to checkout. Hormozi interpreted this as a lesson in identity formation: the girls adopted a new identity (women) and immediately aligned their spending (makeup budget) to match. By allocating their saved money from chores and babysitting to makeup, they were voting for their new identity. This demonstrates that identity shifts require resource commitment (spending and calendar time) before behavior change solidifies.

Hormozi observed that many people say 'I want to own Apple stock' but never purchase the stock. If someone wants to become a wealthy person, they must start 'buying stock in that today' by voting with their dollars and time. This example contrasts aspirational talk (wanting an outcome) with absent resource allocation (no actual spending or time investment), showing that talk without aligned spending does not create identity change.

practices.text: Comment below this video stating what specific action you will take today—not a New Year's resolution, not a future commitment, but something concrete you will do within 24 hours if it is truly important enough to pursue.

Examine your bank account and calendar at the end of each month or quarter, and use these two inputs to determine your true priorities and identity. Compare stated goals to actual spending and time allocation to surface areas of misalignment.

When adopting a new identity, allocate money or calendar time immediately as a commitment device, not after you have been the new identity. The spending or scheduling change should precede the behavior shift.

Invest a portion of discretionary capital explicitly in skills, education, courses, and coaching rather than consumption. Track skill-investment spending separately from stuff-buying to maintain visibility on the wealth-building components of your spending.
